title: Decision Broker and Adaptive Enforcement Layer for Console, API, and Runtime
creator: Asha Patel
description: Build a v2 RBAC decision broker service plus a small adaptive enforcement layer (middleware) that can be wired into the API gateway, runtime request path, and Console. The broker will evaluate compact policy representations, cache decisions for common attribute vectors, and emit structured audit events. The middleware will perform fast-path allow/deny checks, fetch explanatory metadata from the broker for 'explain' traces, and handle fallback modes (deny-open vs deny-closed) controlled by rollout flags.
background: Current RBAC v1 is spread across several services: a monolithic authorizer in the API gateway, ad-hoc guards in runtime, and Console-specific checks. This has led to inconsistent deny semantics, duplicated policy logic, and gaps in audit coverage exposed during a recent incident where a canary role change did not propagate to runtime requests. RBAC v2 aims to centralize policy evaluation while enabling low-latency enforcement paths and richer auditability.
design_decisions: 1) Use a lightweight gRPC decision broker that accepts pre-compiled policy blobs and attribute vectors. 2) Maintain an LRU decision cache with TTL per-policy to support microsecond-level enforcement in the middleware. 3) Represent policies as a small, serializable condition graph (not raw DSL) to speed eval and make caching stable. 4) Emit structured audit events in CloudEvents format to the audit pipeline with correlation IDs. 5) Support 'explain' traces to return reason codes and policy IDs for observability and debugging.
tradeoffs: Centralizing evaluation reduces divergence but increases a single point of latency; mitigated by caching and an adaptive fallback in middleware. Engineering effort vs speed: implementing a serializable condition graph requires upfront work but improves runtime predictability and testability. Stronger audit semantics increase event volume; we will sample 'explain' traces and use policy-level filters to limit noise.
implementation_plan: Phase 1: Broker MVP - gRPC API, policy ingestion, in-memory compiled graph executor, basic audit sink (to staging audit-topic). Phase 2: Middleware - lightweight SDK for API gateway + runtime + Console, local LRU decision cache, fallback modes, metrics and traces. Phase 3: Hardening - HA deployment pattern for broker, persistence for policy versions, SDK language bindings, and rollout automation. Each phase includes tests, a conformance test-suite, and a canary rollout plan.
rollout_plan: Start with internal-only policies for instrumentation and feature flags. Roll out broker to staging region and wire Console middleware in 'audit-only' mode (permit decisions but log discrepancies). Then enable runtime and API gateway in deny-open mode for low-risk roles, followed by progressive tightening to deny-closed for production scopes. Use canary groups, feature flags, and an automated rollback if error rates exceed thresholds.
testing_plan: Unit tests for the compiled graph evaluator; property tests for policy translation; integration tests exercising SDK + broker + audit sink; chaos tests to validate fallback semantics under broker failure; performance benchmarks for cache hit/miss latencies and throughput. Add regression tests derived from the incident that motivated this work.
acceptance_criteria: Broker accepts policy blobs and returns deterministic allow/deny for canonical attribute vectors
Middleware enforces decisions with p50 enforcement latency < 1ms on cache hit and < 12ms on cache miss
Structured audit events contain policy_id, decision, request_attributes, actor, resource, timestamp, and correlation_id
Fallback modes operate as documented (deny-open, deny-closed) and can be toggled via feature flags
End-to-end conformance tests covering Console, API, and runtime pass in staging
